analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional maps with independent citizen commissions instead of legislators.
analysis.headline: The FAIR MAPS Act was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on April 9, 2024, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the drawing of congressional district maps out of the hands of state legislators and give it to a 15-member citizen commission in each state. Members could not be officeholders, candidates, lobbyists, or paid campaign workers, and the commission would have to hold public hearings, publish draft maps, and explain its choices. The bill also bans states from redrawing maps mid-decade, sets standards the maps must meet, and lets any citizen sue in federal court to enforce them.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, especially in states where one party currently draws its own district lines. Competitive elections, communities kept together, and open map-drawing with public input. Members of racial and language minorities protected under the Voting Rights Act, whose ability to elect candidates of choice the bill requires commissions to preserve.

how_it_helps.text: Requires congressional redistricting in every state to be done by an independent redistricting commission of 15 citizens, rather than by the legislature, with a court drawing the maps if the commission fails [S2].
Bans states from redrawing congressional maps again until after the next census, unless a court orders it to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act [S2].

Disqualifies officeholders, candidates, lobbyists, campaign staff, and their immediate family members from serving on the commissions, and requires commission staff and contractors to disclose a decade of political spending [S2].
Requires public hearings, published draft maps, live-streamed meetings, and public comment before a final plan is approved [S2].
Prohibits maps drawn to unduly favor either political party and lets any citizen sue to enforce the law in an expedited three-judge court proceeding [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State legislatures and political parties, which lose their power to draw congressional maps to their own advantage. States also would run the commissions, funded by a federal payment of $150,000 per congressional seat [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the traditional power of state legislatures to set their own congressional districts under the Constitution's elections clause, which critics view as a federal intrusion on state authority; the bill itself includes a section asserting Congress's constitutional authority to impose these terms [S2].

Title V would apply the new requirements retroactively to redistricting done after the 2020 census, forcing states to redo maps already in place for the 2024 elections and potentially throwing them into litigation mid-decade [S2].

The partisan-fairness test relies on quantitative measures such as the efficiency gap and seats-to-votes curve, which are contested methods and could generate years of court fights over whether a map is one seat too biased [S2].
If a commission deadlocks or a state fails to set one up, a federal three-judge court draws the maps instead, replacing one unaccountable process with another [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — taking map-drawing away from the politicians who benefit from the lines — is real and addresses a widely recognized problem, but the bill's design has genuine frictions: retroactive application to existing 2020-cycle maps is legally and practically aggressive, and the quantitative bias tests are vulnerable to litigation. On balance it would make congressional elections more competitive and more transparent, at the cost of state legislative control over map-drawing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, so it died without a vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Wiley Nickel introduced the FAIR MAPS Act on April 9, 2024, with Rep. Zoe Lofgren joining as an original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S2][S4].
The bill attracted one cosponsor in total, and the House took no further action after the referral; sponsor introductory remarks were made on April 29, 2024 [S3][S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it would need to be reintroduced to move again [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and state legislators of both parties keep their power to draw congressional maps to favor themselves and their parties, since nothing changed.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill, so no bipartisan test of the idea occurred [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill strips lawmakers of their power to draw the districts they run in and bans mid-decade remaps, making more seats competitive. Incumbents' interest in keeping safe, self-drawn districts runs directly against voters' interest in competitive elections.
Legislatures lose authority over congressional map-drawing to citizen commissions, and party leaders lose the ability to lock in friendly lines for a decade.

industries.industry: Political map-drawing consultants and data firms
industries.note: The bill would curtail the paid market for partisan map engineering by requiring citizen commissions and banning legislators from considering party affiliation or members' residences, though commissions could still hire outside technical experts.
